label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Peter, thanks for putting the case so clearly. Nine years in payroll means you've seen advances go badly, and a few of your points are right. Brenda, this is mainly for you, because we've been through exactly this.

We're a logistics company, about 340 staff across two depots, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. In February 2025, after pushback from Finance that was almost word for word what Peter has written, we closed our advances. We gave two months' notice and ran one financial literacy session with our SACCO. That's essentially the plan Peter is recommending, so it got a fair try.

**What happened in the six months after we closed**

- Calls from debt collectors and loan apps to our office went from a handful to 61 logged by reception. Some of the apps were ringing supervisors who had been listed as "referees" by staff, so a driver's debt became his supervisor's problem.
- Unplanned absence rose on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager traced at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers "sorting out" loans.
- I had a loader come to me with six apps running at once, borrowing from one to pay the next. It took us four months with payroll to unwind.

I can't prove the closure caused all of it, and I wouldn't claim to. But the timing was hard to ignore, and in September 2025 we reopened with a written policy.

**Where Peter is right**

Some people do start living on next month's money, and Brenda's Finance Manager is right that monthly repeaters are a real pattern. Informal advances, approved case by case in the HR office with no limit written down, are also a bad setup. That's what we had before, and I think it's the real problem in Brenda's description. The answer isn't to remove the advance. It's to remove the informality.

Peter is also right that HR shouldn't be the lender of first resort, and that the hours matter.

**Where I'd disagree**

*"The loan apps are the employee's own decision."* Legally, yes. But the consequences don't stay with the employee. Our supervisors got the phone calls, and the missed runs came out of our operations, not the employee's personal budget. The cost didn't disappear when we closed the scheme. It moved somewhere harder to see.

*"Use the SACCO."* We love ours, but SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and need guarantors. That's no use to a parent whose child is sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. Financial literacy helps too, but when someone is on something like KES 28,000 a month, a session on saving doesn't create an emergency buffer that isn't there. People will borrow somewhere, and the only question is whether it's from you at no fee or from an app at a punishing rate.

*"They adjust."* Some did. Others adjusted by borrowing from apps, and we paid for it in other places.

*"It's HR time."* Only if the process runs through HR. Ours doesn't.

**What the numbers look like with a written policy**

Since reopening we get roughly 55 to 70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. That's about half a million shillings a month going out and coming back at next payroll. Over the year we recovered everything except from two leavers, and the total write-off was roughly KES 14,000. That's the whole credit loss.

Now compare that with the cost of closing: absences, missed runs, 61 logged calls, supervisors pulled into other people's debts, and months of payroll and HR time unwinding one man's six loans. None of it sits in one budget, which is why it never shows up in a forecast. It's spread across operations, fleet, reception and HR. The advance scheme costs are small, visible and sit in one place, which is why Finance can see them and the other costs are easy to miss.

The detail that surprised me most is that our own Finance Manager now defends the scheme. His objection was to the forecast being messy, and a fixed ceiling solves that. The exposure is known in advance, so it's no longer a surprise.

**The shape of a policy you could propose**

This is roughly what we run, and Kiprono's "cap it, put it in writing" is the same idea.

- **Cap:** a maximum of 40% of net pay. This is what keeps the numbers small. It also fits the Employment Act, which limits total deductions to two-thirds of wages, and we check that before approving anything, so nobody reaches month end with nothing.
- **Frequency:** once per pay cycle.
- **Repayment:** in full at the next payroll, no instalments rolling over, and no fee.
- **Approval route:** requests go through the payroll portal, not the HR office. That takes the favouritism and awkward conversations out of it, and takes most of the HR hours with it.
- **Repeat use:** Finance's concern about monthly users is fair, so build it in. We treat repeat users as a signal for a conversation (is something wrong, do they need a SACCO referral or a payroll arrangement), not as a reason to quietly cut them off.

**For the 18th**

Finance can quantify the cost of advances, so you need to quantify the other side too. Before the meeting I'd try to pull together:

1. How many people took advances last year, how many took one every month, and what the total outstanding is at any time. This is likely to show that the problem is a small group of repeaters, and the cap and frequency rules address them directly.
2. Any record you have of loan-app calls, supervisors being contacted, absence around month-end, or staff time spent on debt issues. Even a rough count helps.
3. Your own write-off history, if any. I'd guess it's smaller than people assume.

Then propose a written policy on a trial basis, say six months, with a review. Finance gets a ceiling and a forecast, and you get a way to measure whether it works. That's a much easier thing for a Finance Manager and an MD to say yes to than "we'll keep doing what we do."

Peter, I don't think we're far apart on the goal. Nobody wants staff permanently a month behind, and we want that as much as you do. I just found that closing the window didn't stop the borrowing, it moved it somewhere we couldn't see or manage.

Brenda, happy to answer any questions if it helps before the 18th. Good luck.
